```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7.2, fig.height = 4.6, dpi = 144, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%")
source("figure-style.R")
library(idiographic)
data(srl)
data(submissions)
```

Regression analyses of intensive longitudinal data can be conducted at three
levels, each allowing a different degree of heterogeneity between persons
[@lopezpernas2025].

At the **variable-centered** (pooled) level, one model is estimated from the
data of all persons together. The resulting coefficients describe the average
association in the sample and assume that one set of coefficients adequately
represents every person. At the **person-centered** (subgroup) level, the
sample is partitioned into groups whose members share similar coefficient
profiles, and one model is estimated for each group. At the
**person-specific** (individual) level, a separate model is estimated for each
person from that person's own repeated measures. No similarity between persons
is assumed, and many observations per person are required.

| Question | Function |
|:--|:--|
| What are the pooled and person-specific linear associations? | `fit_lm()` |
| What are the pooled and person-specific binary or count associations? | `fit_glm()` |
| Do within-person and between-person effects differ? | `fit_within_between()` |

The three functions accept a `scope` argument (`"pooled"`, `"subgroup"`,
`"individual"`, or any combination) and fit the selected levels on the same
data, so that their coefficients can be compared directly.

## `fit_lm()`

### Analytic question

`fit_lm()` estimates a linear model at every requested scope and returns the
results in one tidy object. The outcome, predictors, person identifier, and
time column are specified once; the `scope` argument determines how many models
are fitted. When `scope = c("pooled", "individual")`, both the pooled model
and one model per person are estimated. Pooled and subgroup models combine the
occasions of many persons, so their standard errors are cluster-robust
(sandwich-estimated), clustered on the person identifier, rather than
model-based. This ensures that the repeated occasions of the same
person are not treated as independent observations.

### Pooled and person-specific coefficients

The example below predicts daily effort from efficacy and monitoring for the
36 learners in the bundled `srl` data, each observed on 156 days.

```{r lm-fit}
lm_fit <- fit_lm(srl, y = "effort", x = c("efficacy", "monitoring"),
                 id = "name", time = "day",
                 scope = c("pooled", "individual"))
coefs(lm_fit, scope = "pooled")
```

In the pooled model, estimated effort increased by 0.44 points per unit of
efficacy (SE = 0.056) and by 0.14 points per unit of monitoring (SE = 0.050).
Both standard errors are cluster-robust. Because every learner contributes to
the same regression, these coefficients describe an average association that
may not hold for any individual learner [@lopezpernas2025].

### Subgroup evidence

Whether the learners form distinct coefficient types is an empirical question.
`test_subgroups()` compares Gaussian mixture models with one to four components
by the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), where lower values indicate
better fit. A one-component solution is a valid outcome of the
comparison: it indicates that the coefficients are drawn from a single
population rather than discrete types.

```{r lm-subgroups}
subgroup_test <- test_subgroups(srl, y = "effort",
                                x = c("efficacy", "monitoring"),
                                id = "name", time = "day")
subgroup_test
as.data.frame(subgroup_test) |> head()
```

The one-population model had the lowest BIC (213.0); the best two-component
model reached 218.3. The learners therefore did not separate into subgroups,
and a subgroup model would effectively reproduce the pooled model. The
differences between learners were continuous, with no evidence of discrete
types.

### Person-specific coefficients

The individual scope returns one coefficient per learner. Sorting the efficacy
slopes reveals the spread of person-specific associations.

```{r lm-individual}
coefs(lm_fit, scope = "individual", term = "efficacy", sort_by = "estimate")
```

The person-specific efficacy slopes ranged from -0.18 (Ravi) to 0.87 (Lars),
with a median of 0.32. Seven of the 36 learners had negative slopes, and only
eight had a slope within 0.10 of the pooled value of 0.44. The spread of
these slopes contains both true between-person differences and sampling error,
because each slope is estimated from a limited number of occasions.

### Coefficient heterogeneity

`pool_coefs()` separates true heterogeneity from sampling error by fitting a
DerSimonian--Laird random-effects model to the person-specific coefficients
. The function reports the uncertainty-weighted pooled
slope, the standard deviation of the true slopes ($\tau$), and the share of
the observed spread attributable to true between-person differences ($I^2$).

```{r lm-heterogeneity}
pool_coefs(lm_fit)
```

For efficacy, the pooled slope was 0.29 (95% CI: 0.20 to 0.38), the estimated
$\tau$ was 0.25, and $I^2$ was 0.91. Under a normal approximation, the true
slopes of 95% of learners lie between approximately $-$0.20 and 0.78 --- a
range that includes learners for whom efficacy is unrelated to effort. The
pooling and shrinkage vignette covers `pool_coefs()` and `shrink_coefs()` in
greater detail.

```{r lm-plot, fig.height=6.4, fig.cap="Figure 1. Person-specific efficacy slopes with 95% confidence intervals. The dashed line marks the pooled slope; the shaded band covers the interval expected to contain 95% of the true slopes."}
plot_coefs(lm_fit, term = "efficacy")
```

## `fit_glm()`

### Analytic question

`fit_glm()` extends the same three-level framework to binary and count
outcomes through a generalized linear model. The `family`
argument accepts `"binomial"` for binary outcomes, `"poisson"` for counts,
and `"negbin"` for overdispersed counts. Pooled and subgroup standard errors
are again cluster-robust.

The bundled `submissions` data are simulated: 40 learners observed on 80
days, with a binary record of whether an assignment was submitted each day.
The learners belong to two types. For the 20 engaged learners, the log-odds
of submitting rise with daily motivation (true slope 1.2); for the 20
avoidant learners, they fall (true slope $-$0.6). Each learner's slope varies
slightly around the slope of the type, and the `type` column records the true
type.

```{r glm-data}
head(submissions)
```

### Pooled coefficients

```{r glm-pooled}
pooled_glm <- fit_glm(submissions, y = "submitted", x = "motivation",
                       id = "learner", family = "binomial",
                       time = "day", scope = "pooled")
coefs(pooled_glm)
```

The pooled motivation slope was 0.23 (SE = 0.12, $p$ = .057). Averaged over
both types, motivation appeared weakly related to submission --- a coefficient
that describes neither type of learner accurately. This is the expected
consequence of pooling across processes with opposite signs.

### Subgroup discovery

`find_subgroups()` first applies the mixture comparison internally (equivalent
to `test_subgroups()`) and, when a multi-component representation is
supported, assigns each learner to a group. Assignment stability is estimated
through repeated resampling.

```{r glm-subgroups}
set.seed(1)
submission_groups <- find_subgroups(submissions, y = "submitted",
                                    x = "motivation", id = "learner",
                                    time = "day", k = "auto", reps = 30)
submission_groups
```

Two subgroups were selected (BIC improvement of 23.9 over a single population).
The partition coincided with the simulated types for 39 of the 40 learners.
The subgroup assignment then enters `fit_glm()` through the `subgroup`
argument, so that pooled, subgroup, and individual models are estimated
together.

```{r glm-all}
glm_fit <- fit_glm(submissions, y = "submitted", x = "motivation",
                    id = "learner", family = "binomial", time = "day",
                    scope = c("pooled", "subgroup", "individual"),
                    subgroup = submission_groups)
coefs(glm_fit, scope = "subgroup")
```

The subgroup motivation slopes were $-$0.44 and 1.17, close to the generating
values of $-$0.6 and 1.2. The person-centered level recovered the two
processes that the pooled coefficient had averaged away.

### Person-specific estimates

```{r glm-individual}
coefs(glm_fit, scope = "individual", term = "motivation", sort_by = "estimate")
```

The person-specific slopes ranged from $-$1.38 to 1.91. Each learner's model
estimates that learner's slope from the 80 available occasions, with the
precision that sample size allows.

### Coefficient heterogeneity

```{r glm-heterogeneity}
pool_coefs(glm_fit)
```

The random-effects pooled motivation slope was 0.26 (95% CI: $-$0.04 to
0.57), the estimated $\tau$ was 0.79, and $I^2$ was 0.85. The large $\tau$
mainly reflects the distance between the two subgroups: the random-effects
model describes the slopes with a single normal distribution, whereas the
true generating distribution is bimodal.

```{r glm-plot, fig.height=6.8, fig.cap="Figure 2. Person-specific motivation slopes with 95% confidence intervals. The dashed line marks the pooled slope; the shaded band covers the interval expected to contain 95% of the true slopes."}
plot_coefs(glm_fit, term = "motivation")
```

### Assumptions and failure checks

Several conditions determine the validity of the results above.

1. **Independence of persons.** Cluster-robust standard errors correct for
   within-person dependence but assume that persons are independent. Nested
   designs (learners within classrooms) require an additional clustering level.
2. **Sufficient occasions.** Person-specific models require enough complete
   rows per person for estimation and for a meaningful held-out block. Persons
   with too few observations are recorded in the failure table rather than
   silently dropped.
3. **Outcome distribution.** The binomial family assumes a binary outcome
   coded as 0/1 or as a two-level factor. Overdispersed counts should be
   modelled with `"negbin"` rather than `"poisson"`, because the Poisson
   assumption of equal mean and variance produces standard errors that are too
   small when violated.
4. **Coefficient comparability.** Pooling with `pool_coefs()` and subgroup
   discovery with `find_subgroups()` require person-specific coefficients that
   are on the same scale. Differing predictors, coding, or transformations
   across persons invalidate comparisons.

## `fit_within_between()`

### Analytic question

A regression on the raw scores of a repeated-measures variable conflates two
associations: the association between a person's daily deviations from their
own average (within-person), and the association between persons' long-run
averages (between-person) [@saqr2024]. Whether these two
associations differ is an empirical question with substantive implications. A
within-person effect of efficacy on effort describes how effort changes on
days when efficacy is above or below a learner's own typical level. A
between-person effect describes whether learners who are generally more
efficacious also tend to exert more effort.

`fit_within_between()` separates each predictor into its within-person and
between-person parts --- by person-mean centring the raw scores and including
the person means as separate predictors --- and estimates a slope for each
part. The `contextual()` accessor reports both slopes and their
difference, which indicates whether the between-person association exceeds
(or falls short of) the within-person association.

### Contextual effects

```{r wb-fit}
wb_fit <- fit_within_between(srl, y = "effort",
                             x = c("efficacy", "monitoring"),
                             id = "name", time = "day")
contextual(wb_fit)
```

For efficacy, the within-person slope was 0.37 and the between-person slope
was 0.59. The difference of 0.22 (95% CI: 0.01 to 0.42, $p$ = .039) indicates
a stronger association between learners than within them: learners who were
generally more efficacious tended to exert disproportionately more effort than
would be expected from the within-person relation alone. For monitoring, the
within-person slope was 0.17 and the between-person slope was 0.10; the
difference of $-$0.08 (95% CI: $-$0.28 to 0.12, $p$ = .44) was not
distinguishable from zero.

### Visualisation

```{r wb-plot, fig.cap="Figure 3. Within-person and between-person slopes with 95% confidence intervals."}
plot_components(wb_fit)
```

### Assumptions and failure checks

The decomposition requires that variation exists at both levels. A variable
with no between-person variance (ICC near zero) has no between-person
component to estimate; a variable constant within every person has no
within-person component. The `variance_components()` function, described in
the descriptives vignette, reports the ICC for each variable.

The contextual effect is an associational difference, not a causal estimate.
The between-person slope is identified under the assumption that no
time-invariant confounders jointly predict the outcome and the person-level
predictor mean. When that assumption is untenable, the within-person slope
remains identified under weaker conditions (no time-varying confounders),
whereas the between-person slope and the contextual difference absorb
unobserved between-person confounding.

## Choice among the three functions

`fit_lm()` and `fit_glm()` estimate associations at pooled, subgroup, and
individual levels. The choice between the two depends on the outcome
distribution: continuous for `fit_lm()`, binary or count for `fit_glm()`.

`fit_within_between()` separates within-person and between-person associations
in the pooled regression. It addresses the question of whether the relation
observed on days when a person deviates from their own average matches the
relation observed across persons who differ in their averages. A substantial
contextual effect indicates that the raw pooled coefficient is a weighted
average of two different quantities.

Prediction accuracy at the individual level is examined in the prediction
vignette with `fit_ml()`. Subgroup discovery and treatment-effect
heterogeneity are covered in the subgroups and effects vignette with
`test_subgroups()`, `find_subgroups()`, and `fit_effects()`. Coefficient
synthesis and stabilisation are covered in the pooling and shrinkage vignette
with `pool_coefs()` and `shrink_coefs()`.
